metadata.note: The New York City Subway, modeled as a construction chronology rather than as modern service patterns. Each feature is a physical corridor that appears in the year it opened and stays on the map, so dragging the slider shows the network being built: the IRT's single 1904 trunk from City Hall up to 145th St, the Dual Contracts web of 1913-1920s that gave the IRT its 'H' and handed the BRT/BMT Manhattan and Queens, the city-built IND trunks of 1932-1940, unification in June 1940, and the thin postwar additions -- Rockaway 1956, Chrystie Street 1967, Archer Avenue 1988, 63rd Street 1989, Hudson Yards 2015, Second Avenue 2017. Features are labeled with the company that BUILT them (IRT, BRT/BMT, IND, NYCTA, MTA), which is why a single modern train may cross several features. Geometry is real MTA track alignment taken from the agency's GTFS shapes, cut at the historical terminal stations for each stage and simplified to ~6 m tolerance; colors are the current official MTA route colors from the same feed. The Staten Island Railway is included because it is a 1860 steam railroad that became part of the subway fare system; it connects to the rest of the network only by ferry. Elevated railways that predate the subway are in new_york_elevated.geojson.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: All headways are estimated -- no timetable research has been done for any era, and the values here do not vary between the 1900s and today even though service levels changed enormously. Average speed is a flat 30 km/h estimate for every feature, ignoring the express/local distinction that is the whole point of the four-track trunks. The IRT Flushing Line's 1927 extension west to Times Square is dated to the year only; the exact date was not verified. Opening years for the BMT Brighton, West End, Culver, Jamaica, Nassau Street and Myrtle Avenue corridors are approximate Dual Contracts completion years rather than verified single dates, because each was a staged rebuild of an older surface or elevated route. Geometry is modern MTA alignment: where a line was later realigned, rebuilt or extended (the 1904 City Hall loop station, the original South Ferry loop, the pre-1952 180th St-Bronx Park terminal, the demolished inner end of the Myrtle Avenue elevated), the modern track is shown instead of the historical one. Closures are not modeled -- every feature runs to 2026 even where the historical structure it represents is partly gone.
metadata.unification_note: 2026-08-24: the 1940 unification is now reflected on the map. Previously every IRT, BRT/BMT and IND corridor stayed in its builder's colour from its opening year all the way to 2026, which asserted that three private companies were still running the subway 85 years after they stopped. Each of those 44 features now ends at 1940 and is paired with a '-unified' feature of identical geometry in the municipal operator's colour, per CLAUDE.md Rule 4. The City bought the BMT on June 1 1940 and the IRT on June 12 1940; the IND was city-built and city-operated from the start, so for it 1940 ended its separateness rather than changing its owner. IND Sixth Avenue opened December 15 1940, after unification, so it was converted outright rather than split. A 'built_by' property on each unified feature preserves the construction attribution the rest of this file is organised around. CHOICE WORTH KNOWING: the municipal era is carried as one operator -- company 'New York City Transit Authority', with segments naming the Board of Transportation (1940-53), the Transit Authority (1953-68) and the MTA (1968-) -- rather than split again at 1953 and 1968. That matches how this file already treats its existing NYCTA and MTA features, which share one colour and do not split at 1968. Not touched: the New York, Westchester and Boston feature (a different story -- abandoned 1937, the Bronx portion bought by the city and reopened as the Dyre Avenue line in 1941) and the Staten Island Railway.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
